# The Discipline of Wonder: On Paying Attention

I stepped outside this morning with no particular destination, only the vague intention of clearing my head. The air had that sharp, transitional quality of early autumn, not yet cold but carrying a hint of the cold to come. The sky was a washed-out blue, the kind that seems to have been laundered too many times, and the street was quiet except for the distant hum of a lawnmower and the insistent chattering of a squirrel scolding me from a telephone wire. I had my phone in my pocket, its screen dark but humming with the gravitational pull of the entire world—news alerts, messages, the endless scroll of other people’s lives. I resolved not to look at it until I had walked at least a mile. This is a small discipline, but a real one. It is the kind of discipline that society no longer demands of us and that we must therefore demand of ourselves.

The thing about paying attention is that it sounds easy until you try it. We assume that seeing is a passive act, that the world simply enters our eyes and our minds register it like a camera recording a scene. But attention is not passive. It is an act of choice, a constant filtering of the infinite raw material of reality. In any given moment, there are a thousand things vying for notice: the texture of the pavement, the angle of the light, the faint smell of woodsmoke, the memory of an argument from three days ago, the anxiety about a deadline next week, the possibility that it might rain, the ache in the left knee, the sound of a dog barking two streets over. To pay attention is to decide, over and over again, what matters. And in an age of engineered distraction, that decision has become both harder and more essential than ever.

I was not always good at this. As a child, I was what adults called “spacy”—lost in my own head, forever missing the instructions, forgetting where I had put my shoes. But I was also, in my own way, an intense observer. I remember a creek behind my grandparents’ house, a narrow, murky ribbon of water that I would visit for hours at a time. I would squat on the bank, my knees growing damp and sore, and watch the water striders skate across the surface tension. I would turn over rocks to see the crayfish dart backward into clouds of silt. I would follow the delicate trails of caddisfly larvae, each one carrying its tiny house of twigs and pebbles like a hermit crab wearing a log cabin. Nobody had told me to do this. There was no educational outcome, no prize for the child who could identify the most species. It was just the pure, unselfconscious joy of noticing—a joy that most children have in abundance and most adults have to relearn through painful practice.

The creek taught me something that I could not have articulated at the time: that attention is a form of love. To truly see a thing is to care about it, even if only for a moment. The water strider, with its impossibly long legs and its shadow-dappled dance on the surface, became a tiny universe of wonder. I did not need to know its scientific name or its role in the ecosystem. I just needed to witness it. And in that witnessing, I was briefly liberated from the prison of my own thoughts. The creek was a meditation without the word. I was not trying to be mindful. I was just absorbed, the way you are when you are young and the world is still new enough to be endlessly strange.

Somewhere along the way, I lost that absorption. School taught me to value efficiency over curiosity. The constant ticking of clocks, the ringing of bells between periods, the pressure to produce correct answers rather than interesting questions—all of it trained me to see the world as a series of obstacles to be managed, tasks to be completed, deadlines to be met. I learned to move through life with my gaze fixed on the horizon, scanning for threats and opportunities, rather than attending to the ground beneath my feet. I learned to be productive. I learned to be distracted. I learned, above all, to hurry. And hurrying is the enemy of attention. You cannot rush a water strider. You cannot rush a tree. You cannot rush a human being who is trying to tell you something important.

It was not until my mid-twenties, when I found myself burned out and empty, that I began to think seriously about attention as a practice. I had achieved the things I thought I was supposed to achieve: a degree, a job, the vague social approval that comes from being busy and successful. But I felt like a ghost haunting my own life, present in body but absent in spirit. I could not remember what the last three months had contained except for a blur of tasks and screens and anxious thoughts. I was living at the speed of the internet, which is to say I was living at a speed that no human nervous system was designed to sustain. Something had to give.

What gave was my pride. I started doing something that felt embarrassing in its simplicity: I started walking. Not walking to get somewhere, not walking for exercise, but walking for the sake of walking, with no other purpose than to see what I could see. I would go out in the early morning before work, or at dusk, and amble through my neighborhood as if I were a tourist in my own life. And because I had no destination, I had no reason to hurry. I began to notice things that had been there all along: the way a particular brick wall turned gold in the late afternoon light, the three-mailbox cluster at the end of a cul-de-sac where a neighbor had planted rosemary that perfumed the air, the cracked sidewalk where a weed had pushed through with astonishing determination.

At first, these observations felt trivial. What was the point of noticing a weed? But as the weeks passed, I realized that they were not trivial at all. They were the opposite of trivial. They were the texture of existence, the small particulars that constitute a life. We tend to imagine that the important moments are the big ones—weddings, funerals, promotions, disasters—but the truth is that we spend most of our lives in the small moments, and the quality of those moments is the quality of our lives. If we are perpetually distracted, perpetually elsewhere, then we are not really living our lives at all. We are just running a simulation of our lives, our bodies present but our minds adrift in a sea of notifications.

There is a particular oak tree in a park about a mile from my apartment. I have known it for three years now, and I visit it whenever I can. It is not a remarkable tree by any objective standard—not the tallest, not the oldest, not the most beautifully shaped. But I have watched it change through every season, and that history makes it unique to me. In winter, its bare branches etch a wild calligraphy against the gray sky. In spring, it puts out leaves the color of lime sherbet, and the squirrels go mad with the abundance. In summer, it throws a deep, dappled shade that feels like a blessing. In autumn, it burns orange and rust before letting go of everything, dropping its leaves in a slow rain that carpets the ground. I have sat against its trunk on days when the world felt too loud, and I have leaned my forehead against its bark, and it has never once failed to be exactly what it is. That is the thing about trees: they do not pretend to be anything other than themselves. They do not check their phones. They do not worry about the future or regret the past. They just stand in the light and do the slow, patient work of growing.

I know that it is sentimental to attribute wisdom to a tree. But there is a kind of wisdom in simply being present, and trees are masters of that. They remind me that growth is not a sprint. A tree grows a little bit every year, adding a ring that no one can see until it is cut down. It does not strain to become taller. It does not compare itself to the other trees. It just receives what the sun and rain give it, and it makes the best of whatever soil it finds itself in. I would like to live like that. I would like to be less frantic, less hungry for validation, more willing to trust the slow accumulation of time.

Attention is not only a way of seeing nature. It is also a way of seeing people. I think about the conversations I have lost to distraction—the times I nodded along while my mind wandered, the times I reached for my phone in the middle of someone’s sentence, the times I was so eager to share my own thoughts that I stopped actually listening. To listen is an act of generosity, but it is also an act of revelation. When you truly attend to another person, you begin to see the complexity behind the facade. The colleague who seems brusque is actually exhausted. The friend who always jokes is actually grieving. The stranger at the coffee shop, the one you might normally dismiss as background noise, has a whole world inside them—a childhood, a fear, a dream they have never told anyone. Attention breaks down the walls we build between ourselves and others. It reminds us that loneliness is not cured by being surrounded by people but by being truly seen.

I have been trying to practice this kind of attention, and it is hard. It is hard because I am always hungry to be seen myself, always eager to interject my own story, always terrified of silence. But when I manage to set myself aside, when I give someone the full gift of my presence, they often light up in ways that are almost visible. It is as if they had been waiting their whole lives for someone to ask a question and actually wait for the answer. I do not always succeed. I still catch myself reaching for my phone, still feel the itch of my own ego pushing to the surface. But the practice, like the walk, is cumulative. Each moment of attention builds on the last. You train a muscle that you did not know you had, and eventually the muscle begins to do the work on its own.

Art and literature are also forms of attention, or at least they can be. The great writers and painters and composers are people who looked at the world more closely than the rest of us and then found ways to show us what they saw. When I read a poem that makes me feel the weight of a particular morning or the ache of a particular love, I am being invited to participate in that attention. I am being shown that the world is full of meaning if only I am willing to look. And when I create something myself—a paragraph, a photograph, a sketch—I am not producing a product. I am practicing attention, the same way a monk practices prayer or an athlete practices a free throw.

There is a paradox at the heart of attention: the more you notice, the more you realize you are missing. Every time I go for a walk, I see something new, and every time I see something new, I am reminded of how much I have walked past in ignorance. The natural world is infinitely specific. No two leaves are the same. No two sunsets are the same. No two moments are the same, and if you blink, you miss them. This can be overwhelming, even existentially dizzying. But it can also be liberating. It means that there is always more to discover, always more to love. The universe is not a closed box; it is an endless fountain of particulars. Attention is the way we drink from that fountain.

I think about the impermanence of all things, how the oak that I love will someday fall, how the creek of my childhood has probably been rerouted into a culvert, how the people I love will one day be gone. It would be easy to use this knowledge as a reason to despair, to conclude that nothing matters because everything ends. But attention offers a different response. It says that the value of a moment is not diminished by its brevity. A sunset is not less beautiful because it fades. A conversation is not less meaningful because it ends. A leaf is not less perfect because it falls. In fact, it is the very fragility of things that makes them precious. We attend to them because they will not last, and in attending to them we touch something eternal—the sacredness of existence itself.

This morning, after my hour of walking, I stopped at the oak tree. The light was still that washed-out blue, but now the sun was climbing higher, casting long golden shadows across the grass. I put my hand on the bark, which was rough and cool and deeply furrowed, and I closed my eyes. I could feel the faint pulse of my own blood, the slight sway of the tree in a breeze I could not hear, the weight of all the seasons this tree had endured. I did not have a profound thought. I did not have an epiphany. I just stood there, present, a body among bodies, a life among lives, paying attention. And for a moment, that was enough.

The discipline of wonder is not about escaping the world. It is about entering it more fully. It is about choosing, in every ordinary moment, to be awake. The phone will always be there, buzzing with its demands and alarms. The news will always be full of urgency and catastrophe. The to-do list will never be complete. But underneath all of that noise is a quieter reality—a reality of water striders and oak trees and human faces, of small kindnesses and strange beauties, of moments that vanish as soon as they arrive. To pay attention is to say yes to that reality. It is to refuse to let your life become a blur. It is to look at the world with fresh eyes, again and again, until the very end.

I am not good at it yet. I may never be good at it. But I am learning. And the learning itself is a kind of living. So I will keep walking. I will keep noticing. I will keep turning over rocks and watching creeks and listening to my friends. This is the only life I have, and it is made of moments. I want to be here for all of them.
